**Analysis**

The Taylor coefficients of a function with simple poles can be obtained from its partial‑fraction decomposition.  
For a pole at \(a\) with residue \(R\),

\[
\frac{R}{x-a}= -\frac{R}{a}\frac{1}{1-\frac{x}{a}}
         = -\frac{R}{a}\sum_{n\ge 0}\left(\frac{x}{a}\right)^{n}
         = \sum_{n\ge 0}\bigl(-R\,a^{-(n+1)}\bigr)x^{n}.
\]

Hence the coefficient of \(x^{n}\) (i.e. \(d_{n}=f^{(n)}(0)/n!\)) is  

\[
d_{n}= -\sum_{k}\frac{R_{k}}{a_{k}^{\,n+1}},
\]

where the sum runs over all poles \(a_{k}\) and \(R_{k}\) are the corresponding residues.

For  

\[
f(x)=\frac{(2025+x)\ln(2025+x)}{(x-1)(x-2)(x-3)},
\]

the residues are  

\[
R_{1}=1013\ln 2026,\qquad 
R_{2}=-2027\ln 2027,\qquad 
R_{3}=1014\ln 2028 .
\]

Thus  

\[
d_{n}= -\frac{R_{1}}{1^{\,n+1}}
       -\frac{R_{2}}{2^{\,n+1}}
       -\frac{R_{3}}{3^{\,n+1}} .
\]

As \(n\to\infty\), the terms with denominators \(2^{\,n+1}\) and \(3^{\,n+1}\) decay to 0, while the first term remains \(-R_{1}\). Consequently

\[
\lim_{n\to\infty} d_{n}= -\,1013\ln 2026\approx -7712.7983.
\]

The proposed solution omitted the crucial minus sign, yielding a positive limit \(+1013\ln 2026\), which is incorrect.
